headline: President at Oasis Talent Group
topSkills: Social Media • Team Leadership • Leadership • Communication • Talent Management
about:
My career path has taken a few unconventional but powerful turns — each building skills that now fuel my passion for the creator economy. From music and entertainment to e-commerce, logistics, influencer operations, and tech, I’ve consistently focused on driving growth, building systems, and connecting talent with opportunities.

I started young, collaborating with teams tied to Def Jam, OVO Sound, and GOOD Music while organizing influencer-driven events and supporting emerging artists. This early exposure to the entertainment business showed me the power of partnerships and cultural influence.

At 19, I launched multiple Shopify e-commerce brands, scaling one store to nearly $1M in revenue during 2021 and creating a private fund to reinvest in profitable stores. This sharpened my skills in digital marketing, branding, and consumer behavior.

I then worked with Amazon Logistics, studying automation and fulfillment systems during a time of massive global supply chain strain. This experience gave me deep insight into operational scale and efficiency.

From there, I transitioned into the creator economy full-time, leading talent operations at a Snapchat-backed Influencer House with over 275M followers under management. I directed talent growth, brand partnerships, and large-scale content operations while collaborating with celebrities, creators, and leading brands.

Eager to expand my tech and systems expertise, I joined Tesla in Silicon Valley in an independent operations role, focusing on automation, efficiency, and workflow optimization at one of the world’s most innovative companies.

All of these experiences led me to launch Oasis Talent Group, where we help creators monetize effectively, secure high-value brand deals, and build sustainable businesses. Our focus is on creating systems that scale — for both talent and brands.

▶ Focus Areas

Talent Management & Creator Growth: Helping creators monetize their audience, build partnerships, and expand across platforms.

Brand Partnerships: Negotiating and executing campaigns that drive ROI and cultural impact.

Digital Marketing & Sales: Crafting strategies that grow audiences, drive conversions, and maximize lifetime value.

Operations & Automation: Leveraging tech and systems thinking to streamline processes and scale growth.

Relationship Building: Connecting creators, brands, and platforms to unlock new opportunities.

http://www.designspeaking.com/naba-is-in-everyday-actions-operae-event-turin/
DESIGNSPEAKING – “Everyday action”, Turin. Naba, the innovative Arts and Design Academy, has participated in the third edition of the fair-exhibition dedicated to the self-produced design. From November 9th to 11th, in Turin, the students of the BA in Design displayed their seven thesis projects. The “Everyday actions” exhibition explores the role of objects in human lives, the interaction and the relationship between them and the way objects mark human daily life. Sara Ricciardi proposes “Happy Carretto”: by leading the cart to its destination, meter after meter, it produces a certain amount of wool. Agustina Mina and Sara Tulli suggests “Kartique” a modular dress made of “Pretex” paper. It is low-cost and practical at the same time. Anna Tilche through “La mia piccola grande fiaba” presents a surreal and innovative book. A project that puts together parents and kids in a ritual act, the one of telling fairy-tales. István Böjte with “Kopia – modular tableware” manufactures a series of assembled and interchangeable objects for the table. They are made in porcelain and cork. Anna Valsecchi offers “Womby”, a beautiful music-therapeutic crib that reproduces the uterine atmosphere, which aim is to reduce the shock given by the post-birth environmental change. Sebastiano Tonelli with “Melanin” interprets the concept of “window” creating a series of overlapping circular modules of different sizes. Finally, Matteo Morelli and Roberto Pellin, with “Lightframe” project, offers a product between industrial and sculpture, the product that tries to break the traditional typologies of lighting, by the creation of complex structures made of light modules. The exhibition is completed by the work of Dominic Wilcox, that presents  “Everyday Actions Orchestra”, an interactive installation made in collaboration with Naba’s students.

honorsAndAwards.title: Ventura Lambrate - Milan Design Week 2014
honorsAndAwards.description:
Ciao,
We are a group of students attending Nuova Accademia di Belle Arti here in Milan. This is our final year before we graduate with our bachelors degree in design, and we would like to show what we have learned during this time. We call ourselves DIG. DESIGN + INTERNATIONAL + GRADUATES. because all of us come from a variety of countries from all over the word, such as Taiwan, Leb- anon, Norway, The Netherlands, Indonesia and Turkey. Our name also describes our ability to DIG for solutions and answers to make better projects.
The most of us have never shown our projects like this before so this application is very special to us. It is the last year, so this would be a great opportunity to do something together as a class before we leave Milan, to continue our journey within the design world.
Even though we have the same classes, the variety of interests are quite wide. So for this application we all decided on the theme «kitchen». We all have our own product and are responsible for the whole process to reach the final product, with the help of our professor Christian Buzio. Our common goal is to make products that fits together as a collection of objects you can find in the kitchen.
This would make a wonderful experience for us, and would make us grow both as designers and individuals. We would be very happy if you can give us this adventure, and we are looking forward to hearing from you. 
DIG

about:
I build AI and operations platforms that turn fragmented workflows into reliable, production-ready systems — across claims automation, manufacturing analytics, and AI agent design. My work sits at the intersection of product strategy, automation, and execution, where discovery, prioritization, and delivery must translate into measurable operational impact.

At Redo, I helped build a claims automation platform from the ground up, translating complex carrier policies into structured workflows and LLM-assisted decision systems. The platform scaled to 500+ daily claims, reduced manual processing by 40%, and improved resolution quality while maintaining production safeguards. That experience sharpened my ability to operate where ambiguity is high, data is imperfect, and operational reliability matters.

At Carat Industries, I partnered with leadership to drive digital transformation, converting stakeholder inputs into prioritized backlogs, roadmaps, and release plans. Aligning engineering, QA, and business teams improved delivery timelines and reduced operational overhead. Platform clarity and disciplined execution drive predictable outcomes.

At Volvo Group, I led data cleanup, dashboard automation, and standardized process design across safety and quality teams in manufacturing analytics. Replacing manual reporting with structured data systems improved accuracy and shortened decision cycles — reinforcing that product management is system design, data integrity, and adoption, not just feature delivery.

I also led the pivot of Mopshy AI from services to a productized AI automation platform, designing agent-based workflows and retrieval-augmented systems that automated sales operations for 100+ businesses. Through this, I developed strong instincts around MVP definition, experimentation, and scaling automation responsibly.

What ties this together is discovery-to-delivery ownership. I define ambiguous problems, conduct user discovery, write PRDs, prioritize trade-offs, partner with engineering, and ensure release readiness. I build platforms that reduce operational friction, improve decision quality, and create measurable business impact.

If you are building AI-enabled products or operations platforms and value structured thinking, cross-functional alignment, and execution discipline, I am always open to connecting.

Supported $500K in pre-seed fundraising conversations while positioning the product within a $390B+ in-home healthcare market. Established early traction for scalable AI- assisted care coordination.

publications.title: Ecossistema de startups no Brasil: Estudo de caracterização do ecossistema de empreendedorismo de alto impacto brasileiro
publications.description: Escrevi um estudo de caracterização e mapeamento do ecossistema brasileiros de startups, em co-autoria com Vanderleia Radaelli, do BID. Esta publicação detalha duas dimensões de análise do ecossistema de startups brasileiro: os pilares estruturais e os atores principais do ecossistema de empreendedorismo que, ao atuarem de forma inter-relacionada, podem ser vetores de superação dos desafios que persistem no ecossistema. Vale destacar que a caracterização do ecossistema de startups no Brasil foi realizada entre o final de 2018 e princípios de 2019. Desde então, o ecossistema evoluiu, os números ganharam musculatura e mais startups foram alçadas à categoria de unicórnios, o que só corrobora a relevância do tema e o dinamismo atual do setor. O estudo conclui apresentando dois desafios estruturais a serem enfrentados e dez recomendações para ações de fortalecimento do ecossistema de startups no Brasil.

publications.title: A construção de um modelo de acompanhamento da evolução de startups digitais em contexto de aceleração: o caso Start-Up Brasil
publications.publishedAt: USP - University of São Paulo · Dec 18, 2017
publications.description: This research aims to present a methodological model to monitor the evolution of digital startups in acceleration context, based on the case study of the Brazilian public program Start-Up Brasil, that supports digital startups, specifically in the period between years 2013 and 2014. Thus, it describes the model developed by the program and its development process, as well as the main elements present in the literature that have supported it, such as the customer development (BLANK, 2003) and lean startup (RIES, 2011) approaches, among others. The research also contextualized the main concepts related to the thematic, such as startup, accelerator, entrepreneurship ecosystem and innovation habitats. By utilizing both theoretical references and the professional report of the author, who held the position of Operations Director of the program during that period, this work is based on a combination of technical report, descriptive research and bibliographic review methods to then introduce the model. Considering the importance of startups to the development of high impact innovations, especially those related with the Information Technology and Communications (ITC) sector, it is expected that this work can contribute to the development of this area, once that monitoring methods, when well applied, can lead to a better quality of the selection and acceleration of startups, and as a consequence, to the development of the ecosystems in which they are present.

headline: Lovable | Recognized leader by H.M. the King
about:
Sophia holds a B.Sc. in Business & Economics and has been widely recognized for her leadership and entrepreneurial drive across both the nonprofit and for-profit sectors.

Her work spans startups, incubators, venture capital, investment banking, investor relations, social impact initiatives and project management at well-established firms. For her efforts, Sophia has received several national awards, including recognition from His Majesty the King of Sweden and a place on Nova’s list of Sweden’s top 111 talents. Most recently, she was awarded the prestigious Anders Wall scholarship of 200,000 SEK for her entrepreneurial achievements and commitment to positive impact.

With experience in business development, strategy, project management, and corporate relations, Sophia has led teams and built ventures that combine purpose with performance. She brings an entrepreneurial mindset to everything she does, grounded in values-based leadership and a passion for driving change.

headline: On a mission to empower anyone to create.
about:
I'm Anton and I care about having positive impact for the world.

I started Lovable because I believe that democratising the ability to create software is one of the highest levers to unlock more creativity and human potential.

Previously I worked with particle physics at CERN, before joining as the first employee and engineer at Sana Labs, where I helped it succeed in improving the lives of millions of learners and raising $80m+. After this I co-founded Depict.ai, scaled to serve billions of product recommendations and raised $20m from top investors.

publications.title: Second Language Acquisition Modeling: An Ensemble Approach
publications.publishedAt: Proceedings of the Thirteenth Workshop, Building Educational Applications, NAACL 2018 · Jun 9, 2018
publications.description:
Won International competition by Duolingo, showing that we had the best ML methods for understanding learning behavior.

Accurate prediction of students knowledge is a fundamental building block of personalized learning systems. Here, we propose a novel ensemble model to predict student knowledge gaps. Applying our approach to student trace data from the online educational platform Duolingo we achieved highest score on both evaluation metrics for all three datasets in the 2018 Shared Task on Second Language Acquisition Modeling. We describe our model and discuss relevance of the task compared to how it would be setup in a production environment for personalized education.

Adept at building and scaling high-performing technical and non-technical teams and cultures - whether at strategic level or hands-on. Calm under pressure, rapid learner, delivery & results focused, technical and building AI-first, commercially-minded and deeply values-driven.

What I do
- I help founders and leaders navigate moments where playbooks no longer apply - new technology, new scale, or organisational inflection points.
- I take trusted, end-to-end ownership across operations, product, technology, growth, and teams, increasingly using AI-first approaches to reduce complexity and increase leverage.

How I help
- Make sense of ambiguity quickly (signal > noise, root causes > symptoms)
- Turn uncertainty into prioritised action through first-principles thinking and experimentation
- Build calm, scalable operating systems rather than reactive fixes
- Ship real products, tools, and systems - not just strategy
- Leave teams more grounded, capable, and independent than before

When I’m most useful
- When leaders need someone they can trust with the whole system
- When technology or markets have reset the rules 
- When progress needs to be sustainable, not performative

I'm a values driven operator that always strives to bring energy, inquisitiveness, focus, transparency and calmness to teams; as well as being comfortable both at early and later stages.

headline: AI doesn’t produce bad output. Bad operators do. | Technical CRO | Lovable Ambassador | ex-AWS | ex-Microsoft
topSkills: Leadership • Cloud computing • Technology Sales • Go-to-Market Strategy
about:
At AWS I built and led organizations across EMEA. At Microsoft I directed cloud and AI transformation pre-sales across Europe. Then I left and built everything solo with AI. Same skills. Different medium. 

There has never been a better time in history to become a builder. Every resource constraint has been removed. AI can write, code, analyze, design. But it doesn't self-direct and it doesn't know what good looks like. That stays with you.    

Being a builder is not a job title. Not a technical skill. A builder is someone who leads AI with the same rigor a great leader brings to an organization. Clear direction, high standards, and the willingness to iterate until the output is actually right.

The builders who thrive are not the most technically fluent. They are the most operationally rigorous. That is a skill you develop. Not one you either have or don't. 

I write about what it takes to be the person directing it.

headline: AI Travel Tech since 2014  |  Innovation, AI, & Tech Commercialization at Flight Centre |  Former Founder & CEO of Shep (acq.)  |  BTN & Skift Innovator Lists  |  Serial Founder & Advisor
about:
Daniel Senyard leads Compl.ai as they rethink how company's create travel policies and control their second-largest controllable expense. Combining a deep background in digital and social marketing with a strong design and product vision, Senyard is a published writer, sought-after speaker and “product guy.”

During his 11-year digital media and product management career, Senyard has created engaging and unique content, products and digital experiences in industries as diverse as music, real estate, travel and technology. 

From full-scale, national marketing and launch campaigns to niche blogging, editorial writing, podcasting and public speaking engagements, Senyard has done it all. Prior projects and clients include vivogig (founder), Strongpages, Microsoft, Amazon, SXSW and Keller Williams Realty. In addition to his writing and marketing background, Senyard has led cross-industry design and development teams, both local and remote, in mobile, web and print strategy and delivery. Whether managing the UX design of an app, conceptualizing assets for onsite event marketing or guest speaking in classrooms and conferences, Senyard has the technical knowhow and management skills to move any project or product from ideation to delivery.

In his last startup role as founder and CEO, Senyard led the product vision, launch strategy and operational management of the vivogig fan engagement and band discovery platform across mobile apps, the web and widgets.

slides.title: Why I sold my travel startup after it recovered from the travel downturn
slides.subtitle: Daniel Senyard on LinkedIn
slides.description: For most founders, selling your startup is a goal - a dream realized. For many, it’s the end of a long, hard, and winding road. But for the Shep team, the recent acquisition of our startup by travel superpower, Flight Centre Travel Group, is not the end, but a new beginning. The recent acquisition of our startup by travel superpower, Flight Centre Travel Group, is not the end, but a new beginning. Making it as a travel tech startup during COVID has been a massive task that pushed our team to the brink. We lost all of our customers, cut our headcount to the minimum, and pivoted our product. After making those hard decisions, we’ve found great success with our business travel communication platform. In fact, we grew our customer count and revenue to levels that exceeded our early success pre-COVID but we needed to grow much bigger to support all of that activity! Shep team at the Austin Startup Crawl 2017 Startups typically grow through four possible avenues; revenue, fundraising, partnerships, or acquisition. Here’s a little context on why we decided that joining Flight Centre was the right decision for us: Revenue: While we continued to grow our revenue, COVID dramatically elongated the sales cycles while also limiting customer budgets (higher CAC + lower ACV). So, while we were closing customers, we found ourselves having to discount heavily due to limited business travel. Fundraising: Up to 2020, we’d grown primarily through investor capital which allowed us to develop our team, build our product, and find product/market fit. When COVID hit and our existing customer pool dried up, financially-focused (vs. strategic/industry) investors shied away from the travel segment due to the short-term uncertainty. Partnerships: We deepened our partnership with Flight Centre at the onset of COVID. They saw the longer-term picture and opportunity to differentiate, and after two years of close collaboration, it was time to take our partnership to the next level. Acquisitions: Tada! We didn’t sell because we were exhausted by a struggling industry (although we were exhausted). We didn’t sell because we couldn’t get enough customers (we had more than we could handle). We sold because we were excited and wanted to keep our momentum coming out of the COVID travel pause going. We knew that Flight Centre (their FCM division in particular) was the team to help us fully realize our potential and provide us with the resources we’ve been lacking since shrinking the team in early 2020. The Shep team did not sell to get out. We sold to dig in! And we can’t wait to accelerate our progress. The Shep team did not sell to get out. We sold to dig in! Pitching Steve Huffman, CEO of Reddit Long-term partners When my cofounders and I launched our first landing page in 2017, the first chat visitor was from Flight Centre. Before anyone else in the industry had any idea what we were building, Flight Centre was already curious. And that continuing culture of curiosity, innovation, and partnership is why joining forces with one of the globe’s four largest travel management companies (TMCs) was a good fit. Before anyone else in the industry had any idea what we were building, Flight Centre was already curious. We’ve continued to partner with the FCM team as noted in a recent article in BTN’s The Beat, “Having worked together ‘quite extensively over the last couple of years,’ Shep already had been ‘well integrated into our product process,’ said John Morhous, Flight Centre Travel Group chief experience officer.” In fact, their December 2019 investment and ongoing support thereafter fueled Shep during the COVID travel-pocalypse - from product pivot and onto greater customer traction and revenue than we’d seen pre-COVID. Without their support, we likely would have had to shut our doors as our early pilot customers lost budget and froze their travel programs. A great fit Flight Centre put their money where their mouth (chatbot conversation?) was to help us validate our tool and see how it gelled with their customer base by making a strategic investment in December 2019. That timing was obviously very significant as it put some metaphorical gas in our tank just before COVID brought the corporate travel market to a standstill. Layne demoing Shep at GBTA 2019 They—as we—believed that while the industry was struggling, it would come back with very different requirements and expectations. The opportunity to return to travel with tech that communicated priorities and rules, increased traveler efficiency, guided bookers to more sustainable options, and ultimately differentiated their offering was key. So, the team at Flight Centre doubled down on their belief in us, despite travel volumes being at record lows. They continued to push us to customers, give us access to their internal resources and guidance, and fund some of our development. The opportunity to return to travel with tech that communicated priorities and rules, increased traveler efficiency, guided bookers to more sustainable options, and ultimately differentiated their offering was key. Volunteering at Caritas, a local Austin community kitchen In addition to the alignment with regard to innovation and new post-COVID customer expectations, we got to see the cultural fit of FCM. While still in due diligence, they invited our team to join them at customer and team dinners (and late-night Karaoke sessions) while out at GBTA, a large corporate travel industry conference. Sure, it may have confused a few of the employees unaware of the acquisition-in-progress, but they welcomed us with open arms and made us feel like family before we were, nonetheless. They welcomed us with open arms and made us feel like family before we were, nonetheless. The culture of care at Flight Centre affected me personally as—in the middle of due diligence—my mother became gravely ill in South Africa. With the support of both the Shep and Flight Centre teams, I flew to South Africa with my wife and kids where I got to see her before she passed away on December 29, just 7 days after my official start date as an FCM employee following the acquisition. Experiencing the joy and excitement of selling my startup while going through the grief and sadness of losing my Mother touched both ends of the spectrum. I truly appreciate the kindness and patience that I have been shown while I went (and continue going) through this emotional rollercoaster. My wife, Anna; me; my kids; my sister, Amy, and my Mom. What’s next The Shep team will continue building cutting-edge browser extension technology to provide consistent cross-site communication about policies, COVID guidance, sustainability, and preferred suppliers. We’ll continue supporting our FCM and non-FCM customers, but with access to best-in-class resources, data sources, sales, and marketing. While we’ll continue working with our existing customers, we’ll likely be positioned more as an integrated feature of the new FCM platform than a stand-alone product moving forward. We’re excited to keep the story going! Shep winning Plug and Play Travel Demo Day in 2018 We couldn’t have done it without... While Rey Garcia, Layne Cassidy, and I are ecstatic to join the FCM team, we couldn't have done it without our board of Ellen Keszler (ex-President of Travelocity for Business) and Craig Cummings (Moonshots Capital), along with the mentorship, support, and investment by amazing folks including (but not limited to) Moonshots Capital, Capital Factory, Plug and Play Tech Center, MassChallenge, Chris Hoyt, Jimmy, Carolyn, Johnny Thorsen, John Morhous, Marcus Eklund, Mitch Gross, Kathy Misunas, Mariano Dima, Marc Nathan, Pete Harrison, Mike Daly, David Chemerow, Shakeel Rashed, Ben Boyd, Jen Cummings, and most importantly, my wonderful, patient, and supportive wife, Anna Senyard Shep with Craig Cummings, Shep board member and Moonshots Capital partner at the Austin Startup Crawl 2021 We'd also like to acknowledge (and strongly endorse) our prior team members who played critical parts in our growth and development: Skipper Chong Warson, Simon Gooder, Ana DeAlvare, Jeremy Brooks, Ryan Manor, Dan Molitor, Andy Jones, Crystal Rivera, and co-founder, Rafael Torres. For the official press release, check out the FCM blog: https://www.fcmtravel.com/en/press-releases/fcm-fortifies-technology-expertise-through-shep-acquisition

headline: founder of girls in marketing | creator & speaker 🎤  forbes 30u30 | honest conversations about the chaos, courage + ambition behind building a career you love 💫
about:
i’m Olivia, founder of Girls in Marketing, accidental entrepreneur, forbes 30u30, and creator documenting the real side of building ambitious ideas from the ground up.

what started as a small community has grown into a global platform helping thousands of marketers build confidence, find belonging, and create opportunities they once thought were out of reach.
I never planned to run a business (let alone multiple ones!) 
but here we are... and honestly? I wouldn’t change it for the world

over the past 8+ years, I’ve trained over 18,000 marketers, spoken on global stages, and partnered with brands like Adobe and monday.com. but the thing I’m most proud of is building spaces where ambition feels safe and reminding people that success doesn’t have to come at the cost of yourself.

that’s what Ambition is a Dirty Word is all about - exploring the messy middle between drive and burnout, confidence and doubt, growth and rest.

what you’ll find here: marketing, leadership, psychology, ambition, and the unfiltered reality of entrepreneurship - no perfect founder story, just the truth.

if you want to connect, collaborate, book me to speak, or offer me a book deal 😉 
my inbox is always open: olivia@girlsinmarketing.com 🎤💫

headline: AI Solutions Builder | Lovable Ambassador + L5 Diamond | Turning Business Problems into Working Apps | Founder, ThnkLab
topSkills: Artificial Intelligence (AI) • Content Development • Publishing • Executive Management • Marketing Communications
about:
I break things to understand how they work. Then I build them better.

I'm the Founder of ThnkLab and a Lovable Ambassador, and I sit at a rare intersection -- I understand how businesses actually operate, and I know how to build AI-powered tools that solve their real problems. Not theoretical frameworks. Working applications, deployed for real clients, solving real pain.

I've been diving into the unknown for decades. It started in the dot-com era at startups like eToll and Grok Technology, where I taught myself to build because someone had to figure it out. Then 20 years leading marketing, technology, and operations for trade associations -- running teams, managing budgets, owning digital transformation, and learning exactly how organizations resist change and how to move them anyway.

Now I'm building at the intersection of AI and business. Using tools like Lovable, Chipp AI, and Claude, I've delivered custom CRM systems that break even against SaaS subscription costs in under 3 years, AI-powered customer service agents providing 24/7 coverage without adding headcount, and purpose-built applications for clients who don't have a tech team and can't afford to wait for one.

I also bring this work into the room directly, designing and delivering workshops on AI-powered development for non-technical audiences. Topics have included AI 101 for Construction, Vibe Coding with Lovable, Chipp AI and Lovable together, and Building Applications as a Non-Technical User. If you can explain something clearly enough to teach it, you actually understand it.

My edge isn't just knowing how to build with AI. It's knowing which problems are worth solving, how to make the case to decision makers, and how to deliver something that actually works in the real world.

Curiosity over caution. Build over debate. Ship over perfection

If you're working on something that needs both business sense and AI execution, let's talk.

My edge is sitting at the intersection of business strategy and AI execution. I understand the problem before I touch the tools, which means what gets built actually gets used.

Recent results include:

headline: Founder & President @ START Paris | VC Scout | Ambassador @Lovable & VivaTech | Mentor & Speaker | Empowering the next generation of founders & leaders across Paris & Europe
topSkills: Entrepreneurship • Event Management • Networking • Leadership • Global Strategy
about:
My Mission

I build bridges inside the European startup ecosystem so founders move faster than the system around them. Through START Paris, I challenge the French ecosystem with a global perspective, pushing ambition beyond local habits. 

Over the last two years I’ve helped 1,500+ founders, students, and ecosystem leaders access European conferences, investors, and network, but this is only the beginning. 

My goal is to align Europe’s fragmented ecosystems into a coherent pathway for founders, investors, and builders.

What I Do Today
I lead START Paris to open France to international standards and networks. We design events, delegations, and programs that connect young founders with investors, operators, and global opportunities. 

I have mentored startups from Korea, helping them navigate Europe and adapt to new markets, and I supported initiatives such as the launch of EWOR in Paris to broaden pathways into entrepreneurship.

Alongside this, I act as a VC Scout at Growth & Glory and a Lovable Ambassador, helping founders prototype faster and think globally from day one. 

I have also contributed as a one-off speaker at the Founder Harbour Summit in Hamburg, speaking about the startup European ecosystem and as a moderator at Space AI Voice Agents, engaging in conversations at the intersection of AI and entrepreneurship.

How I Operate
Ecosystems are built by people who show up consistently. I organize initiatives that bring together deeptech founders, students, and investors from across Europe, turning Paris into a meeting point rather than a comfort zone. I also like to have calls & meetings rather than texting

My current priority is to make START Paris sustainable and able to thrive without me, with strong teams, playbooks, and long-term partners in place.

Who I Am
French-Danish with years spent in the US, I navigate naturally between cultures and networks. I see Europe as one playground and believe founders should think that way from the start.

Looking Forward
Beyond START Paris, I’m exploring new directions to expand impact across Europe. Ideas are forming, and the next chapter is just beginning, stay tuned.

If you’re building, investing, or rethinking how ecosystems should work let’s connect.

experience.description:
Phase 3 – Rebuild & Delivery (Apr 2025 – Sep 2025):
Led START Paris independently after the previous team transitioned out, ensuring full continuity of the chapter. Organized 7+ events with 20+ partners while personally managing marketing, strategy, partnerships, logistics, and community engagement. Delivered a hackathon with Tech Europe (their first in Paris), introduced Junction Europe’s leading student hackathon organization to the Paris ecosystem, and organized AI Voice Night during VivaTech week, bringing speakers from America, Asia, and Europe together around applied AI and entrepreneurship. 2 days later, hosted Youth of Europe as a continuation of VivaTech, designed to gather the next generation of founders who had attended the conference, with 150+ participants from 15+ nationalities in partnership with Kima Ventures, VivaTech, and other ecosystem actors. Coordinated a European delegation of 6 student founders to TechBBQ, a strategic partner of START Paris, strengthening international visibility. Distributed 450+ VivaTech tickets to founders and students worldwide, enabling broad access to the ecosystem. Recruited and onboarded 15 new team members, restructured internal workflows, and maintained active collaboration with START chapters across Europe to relaunch long-term momentum.

Phase 4 – Structuring for Scale (Oct 2025 – Present):
Currently managing a team of 7 people and building the foundations of the START Paris incubator, set to launch in October 2026. Developing internal playbooks to formalize operations, partnerships, and event execution. Organized the Paris launch of EWOR a leading European venture-building and entrepreneurship education program at Station F, generating 300+ signups and positioning START Paris at the center of high-potential founder creation in France. Led the Road to START Summit in partnership with Inovexus, Lovable, and Village by CA, bringing together 100+ deeptech investors, founders, and ecosystem leaders from 5 countries.

Phase 0 – Research & Foundations (Mar 2023 – Dec 2023):
Visited several START chapters & events across Europe (e.g. Stuttgart, Munich, Berlin, Barcelona) to understand how they operate and grow. These visits shaped the vision and model behind START Paris before its official launch.

Phase 1 – Launch & Partnerships (Dec 2023 – Jul 2024):
Led the early development of START Paris — from branding and positioning to securing our first partners and organizing our launch event (539 registrations, 16+ partners). Focused on building strong local and international partnerships, and running early-stage events.

Phase 2 – International Representation (Aug 2024 – Mar 2025):
Represented START Paris in the global START Network as VP Europe & Latin America. Contributed to international initiatives such as the affiliation program, shared databases, START Recap 2024, and chapter collaboration efforts across Europe and Latin America.

As a Scout at Growth & Glory, I connect with early-stage founders building in climate, deeptech, and AI. My goal is to identify high-potential startups that align with the fund’s mission to support bold and globally scalable solutions that create meaningful impact.

My focus includes:
• Sourcing promising founders across Europe
• Supporting teams through early feedback and warm intros
• Sharing aligned opportunities with the investment team
• Representing Growth & Glory at key events and in founder communities

I listen closely to founders, ask thoughtful questions, and bring a global mindset to every conversation. I’m also continuously learning how to scout more effectively by deepening my understanding of what makes a great early-stage company.
We unite English native speakers with French students. Our goal is create quality connections all over Europe through language exchange.

about:
Most deep tech founders are brilliant at building.

They struggle to make investors believe.

That gap between what a founder has built and what an institutional investor can underwrite is exactly where I work.

I design and deliver founder readiness programs for accelerators and VCs. Not pitch coaching. Structured programs that move cohorts from "we have breakthrough technology" to "here is our market, our traction, our governance, and our ask" — from first check to Series A and beyond.

Conception X. Techstars. Y Combinator. Women TechEU. Female Founders Bootcamp. EIT Supernovas.

What I know from working across hundreds of founders and investors:
The problem is almost never the technology.
→ Deep tech founders have spent years being validated by experts. Translating that into a narrative that holds up in an investor meeting is a learnable skill. I systematize it across entire cohorts.
→ Series A is not a bigger seed round. Institutional investors require financial discipline, governance structure, and a scaling narrative — not just traction. Most VCs don't have in-house capacity to close that gap.
→ US-EU expansion looks straightforward — until a European founder realizes American investors think about risk and GTM entirely differently. I have navigated both sides, operationally and in the fundraising room.

My background:
Chief of Staff at an AI startup in San Francisco → scaled $1M to $30M ARR, team of 30 to 300, raised $50M+ from institutional VCs, led US-Europe expansion.
CPA & former EY auditor → I know what institutional investors look for in due diligence because I have been the person running it.
PhD researcher → I study how deep tech founders build companies that are commercially credible and governance-ready under the EU AI Act.
Guest lecturer on AI entrepreneurship at European universities.
Angel investor in women-led innovation → I evaluate deals, not just advise on them.
—

→ sarahanto.com

experience.description:
Modaal.dev — prompt your way to truly native apps

Modaal is a no-code platform that turns plain-language prompts into production-ready native iOS and Android apps (Swift/Kotlin).
Built for product managers, founders, and boutique agencies, Modaal bridges the gap between prototyping and full-scale native development — without needing an engineering team.

While tools like React Native or Flutter make cross-platform development easier, they often fall short on the native experience: background refresh, offline sync, sensors, camera, widgets, and other OS-level features that define a truly polished mobile app.
Modaal focuses exactly there — the “hard mode” of no-code.

With Modaal, you can:
⚡ Define your app in plain language. Describe UI, data, logic, and monetization flows in natural text.
🎨 Use a built-in native design system. Pixel-perfect layouts and micro-animations built directly in Swift and Kotlin.
🚀 Go from prototype to production. No throwaway MVPs — Modaal apps scale from version 0→1 and 1→100.

We’re on a mission to make native app creation accessible to product minds, not just engineers — empowering teams to ship faster, validate ideas earlier, and own their full product lifecycle.

Founded by Elena Avramenko (ex-Miro, LEGO, Microsoft) and Ivan Misuno (ex-Uber, Meta, Booking), Modaal combines deep experience in mobile infrastructure, AI-driven tooling, and product growth.

Currently in private beta with early agency and founder teams.
📩 Interested in testing or investing? Reach out at modaal.dev
 or message us here on LinkedIn.

slides.title: How to build math practice for kids using vibecoding tool Lovable and ChatGPT
slides.subtitle: Elena Avramenko on LinkedIn
slides.description: Helping your child succeed in math doesn’t have to mean hours of worksheets or expensive tutors. With today’s AI-powered tools, you can create personalized, engaging, and effective math practice at home — even if you’re not a teacher or tech expert. This step-by-step guide shows you how to do it using two simple tools: ChatGPT and Lovable Together, they let you design custom exercises, explanations, and even entire learning experiences — all tailored to your child’s needs. ✏️ Step 1: Start in ChatGPT — Craft the perfect prompt The foundation of a great math practice starts with how you ask for it. In AI terms, that means writing a clear, detailed prompt. Think of a prompt as the recipe you give the AI — the more specific the instructions, the better the result. Here’s how to do it well: 🧠 Be clear about the goal Example: “Create 10 practice exercises for a 9-year-old learning to read analog clocks. Each exercise should include a question, a correct answer, and a short explanation if the answer is wrong.” 📚 Add context about your child Age or grade level Specific topics (e.g., subtraction with borrowing, times tables, fractions) Learning challenges (e.g., ADHD, struggles with word problems) Preferred tone (playful, school-like, competition-based) ✍️ Use examples If you already have an exercise you like, paste it in. The AI will mimic the style and format. Even better — if you have a printout from school, take a photo and include it in your prompt. 🔁 Iterate — don’t expect perfection the first time Your first prompt is just a starting point. Refine with follow-ups: “Make the explanations simpler.” “Add a short hint before the answer.” “Use a space/pony/minecraft theme to make it more fun.” 💡 Extra tips from experienced vibecoders: Treat AI like a collaborator: be direct when it’s wrong (“This is not what I asked, please retry”). Avoid sunk-cost thinking: if a thread isn’t working, start fresh. Try playful roles: “You are a funny pirate teaching fractions.” Kids respond more when AI speaks in character. Think in small asks: instead of a full lesson, request “10 exercises” or “3 hints.” This one-ask-at-a-time principle (also recommended by the Lovable team) consistently produces better results. 🛠️ Step 2: Build and Evolve in Lovable Once you have your prompt, bring it to life in Lovable — a no-code platform that turns AI prompts into interactive learning experiences. How to get started: 📁 Create a project (or add new practice to existed one) For a new project, simply paste your prompt into the search bar and run it. Personally, I keep all practices in a single Math Hub project for my child. It started small — just one practice — and has grown into a library covering clocks, fractions, and times tables. Over time, I layered in more mechanics to make practice stick: ✅ Hints before each question (encourages independence) ✅ Explanations of mistakes (so learning continues after errors) ✅ Small, funny animations (to boost motivation) 🔁 Iterate like a sculptor Add one feature at a time (e.g., hints → feedback → animations). Let your child play, watch how they interact, and refine based on where they struggle. Reuse what works: copy strong patterns and adapt them for new topics. 🌱 What you end up with in Lovable is: ✅ Personalized: Lessons adapt to your child’s exact needs. ✅ Dynamic: You can evolve them as your child grows. ✅ Engaging: Hints, feedback, and animations make practice playful. ✅ Consistent: One hub becomes a long-term learning system. Once you have a test ready, you can even combine topics for mixed practice. ✨ Final Thoughts Creating effective math practice at home used to mean printing worksheets or hunting for the “perfect app.” Now, with vibecoding tools like ChatGPT and Lovable, YOU can design that perfect practice — playful, personalized, and evolving with your child. Start with one small topic — like clocks or subtraction — and build from there. Soon, you’ll have a learning hub your child loves coming back to. 👉 And if you’re curious about what kids themselves can build with AI: check out Memelon.kids — a vibecoded project I created together with my 9-year-old. It helps children learn new words visually, making vocabulary practice just as fun as math.

slides.title: Building memelon.kids: From Idea to MVP in 40 Hours with Lovable + Vibe-Coding
slides.subtitle: Elena Avramenko on LinkedIn
slides.description: For the past 15+ years, I’ve been building products the “classic way” — with engineers, code, and long cycles. And for just as long, I’ve been skeptical about no-code/low-code tools. Could they ever produce something close to the quality and user experience I expect? As someone who’s worked with some of the best designers in top companies, I was extra skeptical about what outcomes these tools could really deliver. Over the last 4 months, I started experimenting with Lovable. At first, I only used it for landing pages and quick prototypes — just a way to visualize ideas. But I never pushed all the way to a fully working product. So I gave myself a challenge: 👉 Take a simple but real use case, and in ~2 weeks (40–50 hours total), build the first version to start validation with real users — without coding skills. 👉 Work as a PM + Designer duo, using Lovable + ChatGPT, and a bit of what I now call vibe-coding (building through prompts, iteration, and creativity). Here’s what happened. The Product we build memelon.kids - a Quizlet-like app for kids aged 6–12 to memorize words using games, fun visuals, and voiceover. The idea came from my own experience. Every two weeks my son brings home a list of 10–15 Dutch words. He needs to know both spelling and meaning, and it’s always a struggle. Before memelon, we cut up pieces of paper with pictures, words, and definitions, and played a physical matching game. Fun, but messy. With Memelon, we have a kid-friendly version of Quizlet - ✨ More fun; ✨ Easier for kids to use; ✨ With the option to create their own practice without parents Step 1 – Ideation Here my process didn’t change. I always start with a simple question to reply: WHAT: Problem to Solve WHO: Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) & Persona WHY: Defensible Differentiation HOW: Strategic Focus I usually capture everything in a structured table. But recently I created a custom GPT - “Pre-Lovable - think deeper before you build” to move through this stage quickly. Feel free to use it. Step 2 – Landing Page Before Lovable, I had a habit of writing a press release first. It forces clarity and creates a future story to aim at. Now, I take my ideation results → refine it in ChatGPT → drop a polished prompt into Lovable. In minutes, I get a landing page. At this stage, page is just a picture, nothing worked — it was just a pretty shell. But it gave the project a sense of reality and progress. Step 3 – From Landing Page to Ugly Prototype Time to make it functional. It takes a lot of small steps to set every piece of your project so it works the way you envisioned. Your goal here is simple: make your landing page work. In my case, I spent most of my time on: Enabling Supabase (first time — doable with Lovable + their chat support). Integrating ElevenLabs , ChatGPT , Stripe , and Pixabay . Building a spaced-repetition system for memorization: when a child learns a word, it moves between “baskets” and reappears after a set number of days. My approach was consistent: 💡 use ChatGPT for brainstorming and shaping ideas, then send only the final refined prompt into Lovable. This saved both time and credits. The result: a fully working prototype. By my standards? Generic, ugly UX/UI. But it solved the core problem. And all the ugliness worked. Step 4 – Human Designer Touch This is where my designer joined in. The transformation was immediate: from hacky demo → “this could be a real product.” Her process and insights: 1. Start Big Lock design tokens first (colors, typography, spacing, radius). Put tokens + rules in a Knowledge Base for one source of truth. Apply design system globally, then refine screen by screen. 2. Keep Prompts Short & Precise Provide context: where, what, how. Add examples. 3. Iterate Incrementally Use chat to clarify why something looks off before fixing. Refine step by step instead of dumping long specs. ✅ What worked: Tokens & global styles applied consistently. Small UI tweaks were fast and reliable. ❌ What didn’t: Responsive resizing was painful, lots of trial & error. Using GPT to rewrite prompts sometimes lacked context — often I had to refine directly in Lovable’s chat. Step 5 – Tech Check Once we had something solid, I showed the MVP to my technical co-founder. His role: identify flaws and help fix the biggest risks. Honestly? He cursed the tools a lot. From the inside, the results felt “messy” to him. But together, we patched some of the critical issues. Step 6 – Release 🚀 And just like that, in ~14 days and 40–50 hours total, we went from idea → landing page → prototype → polished MVP → release. Key Insights Lovable is not a designer. The output without design polish is obviously AI-generated. But Lovable is a multiplier. Combined with ChatGPT for ideation and Figma for design, you can build at serious speed. Product + Design still matter. No-code gives you functionality, but only product sense and design make it memorable. The “ugly prototype” stage is gold (even though I hate it). A working-but-rough version beats a perfect Figma file every time. A PM + Designer duo can now do what once required engineers. That’s a big shift in startup dynamics. What Could Be Better Collaboration: Lovable still feels like a solo tool. Working in parallel with a designer is clunky — you wait for prompts to execute before pushing your own. Stripe integration: works one day, breaks the next. Not fixable via prompts alone. Randomly painful! Sharing sets: I gave up and asked my co-founder to fix it. Right now, the flow for copying a shared set as a non-registered user is too complex. Some non-typical flows - needs manual fixes. Final Thought This was my first real end-to-end no-code/vibe-coding build. It didn’t just help me start validating my idea — it also validated a new way of working: a product–designer duo empowered by AI. The tools aren’t perfect. But the speed and possibilities are undeniable.

slides.title: A B2B vertical that automatically unlocks new distribution channels!?
slides.subtitle: Elena Avramenko on LinkedIn
slides.description: How companies like Miro's, Notion, Webflow use Consultants & Agencies to unlock massive #PLG growth Why Consultants & Agencies vertical is so special Many large enterprises rely on professional service providers, such as consultants and agencies, for various projects. Imagine these providers not only using your product but integrating it into their client projects. This transforms them from mere customers into advocates for your product, introducing it to large enterprises without any direct solicitation from us. This is truly remarkable. The Consultant and Agencies vertical serves a dual role: they are both a client vertical and a distribution channel. This vertical checks multiple boxes for contributing to PLG: Multiplying Reach: Consultants routinely incorporate your product into their work, showcasing it to their clients in the process. Enterprise Gateway: These professionals, even at smaller scales, often engage with enterprise-level clients, offering a valuable entry point. Annual Client Refresh: Given the nature of consultancy, professionals frequently onboard new clients, expanding the potential for product adoption. Starting Point for Enterprise Adoption: It sometimes only takes one successful consultant project to initiate broader enterprise adoption. So, essentially, this vertical not only contributes direct revenue but also drives indirect revenue from the clients they influence. Direct Revenue: This comes from ARR generated by consultants' paid subscriptions (both HT and SS). Indirect Revenue: This is the ARR from paid accounts influenced by external consultants domains. This vertical, therefore, plays a crucial role in broadening your product reach and influence within the enterprise sector, making it an invaluable part of your growth strategy if it goes to ENT. Major clusters within this vertical This group usually called as Professional Service Providers (PSP), and the definition is: "Professional Service Providers (PSP) is an umbrella term used to refer to companies with knowledge workers, that use their expertise to provide bespoke services to their clients." However, it's essential to recognize that not every consultant or agency will boost your product's growth. To find the best partners - dive into our product usage data, looking for patterns. Use analysis to identify certain types of consultants and agencies that are a particularly good fit for you. It can be Architecture firms, Management consulting, IT consulting, Marketing and advertising agencies, Design agencies. After you can categorize these into main clusters based on size: Individuals and Small to Medium-Sized Firms: These should be approached in Self-Serve (SS) way. And Large Firms: These were classified as part of the High Touch (HT) approach. This clustering helps you to customize our approach for each group, maximizing growth and partnership potential. Common strategies to try for this vertical Here are some strategies you can use: 1. Special Pricing Plan: This is a common approach, particularly effective when consultants are among your early adopters. A special plan is justified if their use cases differ significantly from other customers, and your current offerings don't meet these unique needs. 2. Marketing Partner Program: Creating a marketing partner program tailored to this vertical is a straightforward yet effective approach. The first step involves conducting thorough research on various consultants to identify 3-5 benefits that would provide the most value to them. These benefits can be diverse, ranging from features within the product, like unique functionalities or free seats, to benefits outside the product, such as co-marketing opportunities, exclusive onboarding materials, and invitations to special events. This model of a marketing partner program benefit such companies as Notion, Mailchimp, Asana and Webflow Experts. Each of these programs has its own flavor, tailored to the specific needs of the company and its partners, but the underlying principle remains the same: creating mutual value that drives growth for both the company and its consultants or agency partners. 3. Consultant Community: Creating a dedicated community for consultants allows them to share their expertise, engage with each other on collaborative projects and enhances their engagement with product. 4. Collaborate on Content Creation: Consultants, in their thought leadership activities, often produce various types of content such as videos, articles, and case studies, even without being prompted. Content creation is part of their strategy to generate demand for their services. They naturally feel inspired to create content as it showcases their expertise and how they utilize your product. The range of content they produce is usually diverse, including practical case studies, "how-to" articles, both short and lengthy videos, and also templates. What to keep an eye on while building this motion Clarity on Ownership: The professional services vertical isn't a one-department endeavor; it demands coordinated efforts across the company. Establishing this clear ownership and aligning our leadership team to prevent strategic missteps. Focus on One Thing at a Time: It's a classic mistake of having too many irons in the fire can dampen the potential for growth. Resist the allure of pursuing every new opportunity and instead focused our resources on nurturing key areas within the consultant and agency space. This focused approach proved crucial in enhancing the effectiveness of our efforts. Preventing Analysis-Paralysis: Take agile, iterative approach VS to a cycle of endless analysis, which imped progress. Maintain a rapid learning pace, embrace the inevitable setbacks, and avoid getting mired in indecisive analysis. Patience in Community Building: Cultivating a community, particularly with professionals like consultants and agencies, requires a long-term commitment. These relationships need to be developed organically and cannot be hurried or approached transactionally. Genuine community building involves nurturing authentic connections, consistently providing value, and patiently fostering these relationships over time. Patience and perseverance are crucial, as the most substantial communities are built on a foundation of trust and mutual benefit. Conclusion: Harness mutual growth The success of consultants with their clients directly mirrors your success with those same clients. This interconnection is why I find this vertical particularly compelling. The more proficient consultants are in using our product, the broader the exposure and adoption among enterprise clients. It’s a genuine win-win scenario for both our company and the consultants, a dynamic that is drawing increasing attention from many new B2B PLG products. They recognize the value of this vertical and are actively engaging with it. The essence of consultants and agencies is their inherent ability to be vocal and viral about the products they use. Your aim is to magnify this trait. Their role extends beyond mere usage; they actively enrich the product’s ecosystem, bringing in valuable perspectives, resources, and a wealth of practical applications. Their contributions, from in-depth templates to real-world case studies, elevate the product’s utility for all users. Example of non-sponsored video casestudy created by one of Miro Experts In summary, engaging effectively with consultants and agencies is a great part of strategy in your PLG journey. It’s an investment that goes beyond immediate returns, laying the foundation for long-term growth and establishing your product as a staple in the professional landscape. If you’re finding this article valuable, consider sharing it, or subscribing to my Substack if you aren’t already. Sincerely, Elena

about:
After watching hundreds of startup pitches and reviewing endless slide decks, I realised we first need to fix the most basic problem. Everyone is Fake-Building.

If you can replace "market analysis" with "actual revenue," you reverse the entire startup cycle. I didn't write a book (yet), but I co-founded the antidote that fixes this problem: [Habitat] (www.joinhabitat.eu).

And then I realised the following: 'It is not because you have a great idea, that you have a business'. So we designed a format that forces the only metric that matters: SPEED.

In the meantime, I’m scaling Habitat (we take you from idea to validation in 4 hours) and serving as a Lovable Campus Leader (educating people on the latest AI developments). I believe in walking my talk—literally building alongside our cohorts, so check my projects and judge for yourself.

If you're not convinced yet, here is the serious shizzle:

I believe extreme bias for action is the only way to create greater equity value in your business or startup.

Things I (love to) do:

- Helping founders kill their slide decks and build actual products.
- Obsessed with designing environments where you can launch a startup in one evening.
- Building communities of "doers" who value shipping code/product over planning.
- Defining the blueprint for rapid experimentation & building the infrastructure for scale.
- Connecting the most ambitious aspiring founders across Belgium to solve real problems, right now.

Here is a list of ecosystems and partners we are accelerating, feel free to join them: Vlerick Business School, KU Leuven, Ghent University, Solvay Business School, Start it @KBC, Tectonic, Lovable and a growing list of builders who stopped planning and started shipping.

My name is Lucas DiPietrantonio. I lead a powerful team that is leading the future of consumer marketing.

DARKROOM:

- Forbes 30U30 Recipient Marketing & Advertising North America (2024)
- Inc 5000 2023 Fastest Growing Private Companies in America (#358)
- Top 1% Varos Performance Marketing Agency (2023)

Darkroom is a progressive omnichannel growth marketing agency focused on retail, e-commerce, and consumer businesses. 

We help high-growth commerce companies with Marketplace Management, Retail Media, Digital Strategy, Paid Media, Creative, and Overall Revenue Growth.

We opened eight years ago, and now have over 110 people across hubs in New York, São Paulo, Lisbon, and Barcelona. Our team has been responsible for over five billion dollars in trackable revenue for hundreds of commerce, retail, software, and B2C businesses. Using research aggregated across these engagements, we accelerate results for our portfolio by developing high-impact digital strategies that unlock gateways to revenue growth, transform marketing operations, and prioritize profitability.

Darkroom works with many of the fastest-growing companies across industries in the United States. My personal client list there includes Crate & Barrel, Olipop, Necessaire, Dwayne Johnson, and many more. On average, our strategy-driven approach increases marketing efficiency by 25% and reduces aggregate marketing costs by 30%.

INVESTMENTS:

Across our client work, I’ve been fortunate enough to invest in and advise some of the fastest-growing startups in the world through our venture vehicle Darkmatter. My shortlist includes commerce technology platforms like Loveable, Triple Whale, FERMAT, Canal, and InHouse, consumer products like Brami, Evolv, and Sauz. Many of our investments are personal clients or advisory relationships of mine. 

I also was a co-owner and partner of Tejesta, a luxury eyewear brand based in Miami. I exited my position in that business at the end of 2025.

My work has been featured in Forbes, Ad Age, Entrepreneur, Adweek, and in several other notable publications.

I write about my experiences scaling Darkroom, investing in high-growth commerce businesses, and optimizing my lifestyle for peak-performance.

Learn more about me: https://lucasdipietrantonio.com/

Mein Schwerpunkt lag dabei auf der Analyse und Entwicklung von Strategien für Institutionen des öffentlichen Gesundheitswesens wie Ministerien, Ämter und Kommunen.

OptiMedis wurde 2003 gegründet und ist heute Marktführer in der Entwicklung und Umsetzung innovativer Versorgungsformen. Ziel ist es, eine faire und bessere Gesundheitsversorgung zu schaffen – auch über die Grenzen Deutschlands hinaus. Notwendig ist dazu der Fokus auf den einzelnen Gesundheitsnutzen (Value)  und nicht – wie in heutigen Vergütungssystemen – auf die Leistungsmenge (Volumen). 

Im Rahmen meines dualen Studiums war ich Projektmanager in der Abteilung "Research & Innovation" und war dort für EU-Forschungsprojekte mit dem Fokus auf Digitalisierung und innovativen Gesundheitsinterventionen für Patient:innen verantwortlich. publications.title: Generation Alpha: Die Zukunft der Zukunft
publications.description:
Die Generation Alpha wächst in einer Realität auf, in der digitale Technologien, KI, globale Vernetzung und der Klimawandel keine abstrakten Trends sind, sondern Teil des täglichen Erfahrungsraums. Diese frühen Prägungen werden ihr Verhältnis zu Gesundheit, Arbeit, Lernen und gesellschaftlichem Zusammenhalt entscheidend formen. Dabei entstehen zwischen individueller Selbstoptimierung und kollektivem Verantwortungsbewusstsein allerdings sehr unterschiedliche mögliche Lebenswelten. Genau diese Spannbreite gilt es zu reflektieren, um zu verstehen, mit welchen Erwartungen, Werten und Verhaltensweisen die Alphas wahrscheinlich aufwachsen werden.
Für das Gesundheitswesen bedeutet das: Die nächste Generation wird mit einem neuen Blick auf Gesundheit, Technologie und Nachhaltigkeit aufwachsen. Wer heute in Versorgung, Führung oder Politik Verantwortung trägt, kann diese Zukunft aktiv mitgestalten. Dazu muss früher verstanden werden, welche Denk- und Arbeitsweisen die Generation Alpha prägen werden und welche Chancen daraus für ein modernes, resilientes Gesundheitssystem entstehen.

publications.title: Young Professionals im deutschen Gesundheitswesen: Auf der Suche nach Licht im Leadership-Tunnel
publications.description: Die Gesundheitsbranche erlebt einen umfassenden Wandel, getrieben von finanziellen, politischen und gesellschaftlichen Veränderungen sowie der rasanten digitalen Transformation. In diesem dynamischen Umfeld stehen Führungskräfte und junge Mitarbeitende vor der Herausforderung, sowohl Fachkompetenz als auch Methodenkompetenz zu demonstrieren, um sich den rasch ändernden Anforderungen erfolgreich anzupassen. Besonders hervorzuheben ist die aufstrebende junge Generation, darunter die Generation Y (auch als Millennials bekannt) und Z. Diese Altersgruppen bilden einen entscheidenden Teil der Gesundheitsarbeitskräfte. Da viele erfahrene Fachkräfte in den Ruhestand gehen, wird die jüngere Generation eine entscheidende Rolle bei der Aufrechterhaltung der Branche spielen.

slides.title: Anti-Patterns: Dead Code & Lava Flows
slides.subtitle: Jon Higginbotham on LinkedIn
slides.description: In this article we'll look at the definitions and problems of two software development anti-pattern cousins; Dead Code and Lava Flows. We'll go through their dangers if left to grow, their causes, and If you bear with me until the end, I'll provide solutions to both. Since my last article was about the ice cream cone anti-pattern, it's only fitting that now I explore the other end of the temperature spectrum, not to mention the theme fits Halloween rather nicely. But first, let's review what an anti-pattern is: "An anti-pattern is a common solution to a recurring problem that is ineffective or counterproductive. It is the opposite of a best practice and often leads to software that is difficult to understand, maintain, and extend." - Teamhub Blog There are many anti-patterns, and eventually, I hope to write about all of them. I'll do my best to highlight them in the context of low-code (Mendix). The patterns themselves are often universal, regardless of language or platform, though some are more specific than others. Many anti-patterns are consequences of our ways of thinking—fallacies we fall into when making decisions about how we develop solutions. Dead Code Dead code consists of parts of your codebase that are either never called or do nothing useful. Essentially, it's anything that contributes nothing. Examples of dead code include microflows that are never invoked, variables that are never used, or pieces of logic that sit unused. One could argue (and I do) that one-time-use scripts become dead code the moment they've been run. Dead code is bloat; it’s codebase litter—pieces of code that someone didn't remove, either out of ignorance or fear. Courtesy of ChatGPT Causes Dead code is often created by accident and rarely intentional. It’s not always code that is unreachable but may simply never be invoked due to a condition before it (e.g., feature flag or decision split). Forgetfulness, disorganized workflows, and undisciplined practices are all prime suspects. Developers might knowingly create dead code due to tight deadlines, perhaps with the intention of coming back to clean it up later—but we all know how the tech debt story goes. Feature removal: When features are deprecated or removed, developers may leave related code in place. Refactoring: During code refactoring, some parts of the code may become unnecessary, but they might not be deleted immediately. Poor code management: Lack of proper code reviews and cleanup can lead to the accumulation of dead code over time. Hoarder syndrome: "But what if we'll need it in the future" Examples: Excluded microflows/pages that are forgotten. Variables or parameters that have no use. One-time-use scripts that stay forever. Code tied to a feature flag that should be removed. Problems Just like litter or a dirty bedroom, the impacts of dead code aren't readily apparent until it grows to an overwhelming size. Ultimately, it just gets in the way of everything, creating unnecessary time sinks, confusing developers, and contributing nothing positive. Increased maintenance costs: It makes the codebase more difficult to understand and maintain, as developers must sort through unnecessary parts. Bugs & confusion: Dead code might unintentionally interact with other parts of the system or cause confusion. Larger codebase: More code means higher complexity and longer compilation times, even if the dead code isn't actually used. Lava Flows I'm not talking about the sinfully delicious Hawaiian frozen cocktail, but maybe the next time you're tasked with refactoring a code lava flow you do so with one of those in hand (not recommended, but probably pretty fun). Much like its geological namesake, the Lava Flow anti-pattern represents code that’s built up over time, hardened in place, and impossible to move or refactor without significant risk. Lava Flow occurs when dead code, obsolete design elements, and legacy structures remain embedded in a system, even though they no longer serve a useful purpose. Often, these remnants were introduced during rapid development phases, experimental implementations, or early versions of the software that were never properly cleaned up. Over time, these "fossilized" chunks of code become difficult to remove without potentially breaking the functionality of the overall system. Typically these pieces have no documentation, it's generally unclear how they work or what it exactly does, but somehow the system works and therefore, just like a real lava flow everyone is afraid to touch it so instead of refactoring they they build on top of it. Symptoms of Lava Flow Obsolete Code: Old methods, functions, or classes that are no longer used but have not been removed. Unclear Ownership: Parts of the codebase that no one on the current team fully understands or can explain. Usually someone wrote it long, long ago. Increased Complexity: Over time, as the codebase evolves, unnecessary complexity grows, making it harder to introduce new features or refactor existing ones. Fear of Change: Developers become hesitant to modify certain parts of the code due to the risk of breaking the system, leading to stagnation. The Risks of Ignoring Lava Flow Leaving these hardened chunks of code in place comes with significant risks: Reduced Agility: As more "lava" builds up, adding new features or refactoring becomes an uphill battle, slowing down the pace of development. Higher Maintenance Costs: Debugging and maintaining a bloated codebase is more time-consuming and error-prone, leading to higher costs over time. Technical Debt: Every time a developer works around a legacy block of code instead of addressing it, the technical debt grows, making future development even harder. Solutions CULTURE If there’s one thing I hope you take away from these solutions, it's this: Being a real professional software developer means taking ownership not only of the code you write but also the code you inherit. When you see something broken or inefficient, it’s not 'someone else's problem'—it's an opportunity to step up, fix it, and leave the codebase better than you found it. Responsibility in software isn't limited to your own contributions; it extends to the health of the entire system. Regardless of your role, experience, or title, you can inspire others by setting the example—doing the right thing yourself. If you consider yourself a professional, or aspire to be one, excellence must be your standard. That means not allowing bad code to go unfixed or uncleaned. To combat anti-patterns, fostering a culture of refactoring, optimization, and leaving code better than you found it is crucial. This is the hardest challenge because it starts with the individual, and often, people only take it up once they’re inspired by someone else. Maybe that someone is you, dear reader. Instilling this kind of culture in your engineering department or you team is hard. Damn hard. The easiest remedy I can come up with is to lead by example. The benefits of maintaining clean code are not immediately rewarded, it takes learning to love what initially feels like a drag. UNIT TESTING To address the risk of refactoring and removing code, there's really only one valuable answer: automated tests, namely unit tests. Nothing will give you more confidence in touching code you know nothing about. If the codebase you've jumped into has no tests, I feel for you—but let the practice start with you, for the developer who comes after. Imagine working on a project where you could confidently change any piece of code, knowing the unit tests have your back—immediately alerting you if anything breaks. It may sound like a pipe dream, but it’s not as far off as it seems. The first step towards that level of confidence is to start building unit tests today. OWNERSHIP Ensuring that each part of the codebase has a clear owner is essential for maintaining its long-term health and quality. A designated owner takes responsibility for understanding, maintaining, and improving that section of the code. This ownership doesn't mean exclusivity—other developers can contribute—but it ensures accountability. Code ownership empowers developers to take pride in their work while fostering a collaborative environment where accountability and shared responsibility keep the entire system healthy. True code ownership isn't just about maintaining and improving your code while you're there; it's about preparing it for the next developer who will take it over Also, consider this: as a developer, it's almost certain you'll move on from your current project to another at some point. True code ownership isn't just about maintaining and improving your code while you're there; it's about preparing it for the next developer who will take it over. Think of yourself as the caretaker of a "code child"—whether it's a small component or a large system. Your responsibility is to nurture it, clean it up, and make it as resilient as possible, so it's ready to thrive long after you're gone. Write code today that future developers will thank you for. DEBT TRACKING There are realities we can’t avoid, no matter how idealistic we are. Sometimes, despite our protests, we simply aren’t given the time to do things the "right" way, or we lack the personal bandwidth or know-how to fix what we come across. The best way to manage technical debt—other than preventing it altogether—is to shine a light on it. That means documenting and cataloging it so you can (hopefully) sprinkle some debt management into your sprints later. If you don’t add debt to your backlog, it will quickly be forgotten. Conclusion Anti-patterns like Dead Code and Lava Flows are common pitfalls that seem harmless because after all the application may still be working correctly but over time they do more damage to a application than most bugs ever could. However, these patterns don't have to be inevitable. By fostering a culture of ownership, refactoring, and unit testing, we can transform these challenges into opportunities for growth. It starts with each of us taking responsibility—not just for our own code, but for the health and quality of the entire system. Clean, maintainable code doesn’t just benefit today’s project; it sets the stage for the next developer and the future of the application. Tackling technical debt and embracing best practices is no easy task, but it's the hallmark of a true professional. The road to a better codebase begins with a single step, and that step starts with you.
